title: Soil and minespoil fill as media for renovation of nitrogen and phosphorus in domestic wastewater
authors: Peterson C.E.; Reneau R.B.; Hagedorn C.
keywords: Alternative on-site wastewater treatment and disposal systems | Fill material | Low pressure distribution systems | Minespoil | Nitrogen | Phosphorus | Wastewater renovation
abstract: Development of Appalachian coal mining regions of the USA has been severely hampered by lack of domestic waste disposal technologies suited to fills. The suitability of on-site wastewater treatment and disposal systems (OSWTDS) in fill material is uncertain due to the effects of surface mining on soil physical properties. This research was conducted to evaluate the potential for renovation of N and P present in domestic wastewater by fills produced from mining operations. Nitrogen and P were chosen because of their potential adverse environmental impacts. Soil-fill (a mixture of Jefferson, fine-loamy, siliceous, mesic Typic Hapludult and Muskingom, fine-loamy, mixed, mesic Typic Dystrochrept soils) and minespoil (spoil)-fill (blasted rock material associated with the Taggart Marker and Low Splint Bench coal seams of the Upper Middle Wise Formation) were used in this study. Septic tank effluent (STE) and sand filter effluent (SFE) were applied to spoil-fill columns at four loading rates (0, 5.4, 10.8, and 21.6 L m<sup>-2</sup> d<sup>-1</sup>) and spoil-fill columns at one loading rate (21.6 L m<sup>-2</sup> d<sup>-1</sup>) for a period of 20 wk. Renovation of wastewater was assessed by determining the concentration of N and P present in column leachate. Reduction of inorganic N (NO<inf>3</inf><sup>-</sup> +NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup>), based on N/Cl ratios, ranged from 14.9 to 32.1% after the varying application rates of STE and SFE passed through the soil columns. However, leachate NO<inf>3</inf><sup>-</sup> -N concentrations were still above the 10 mg<sup>-1</sup> drinking water standard. The quantity of P emerging from the spoil-fill columns (3.0 mg P L<sup>-1</sup>) was higher than anticipated and may be related to the indigenous P present in the minespoil. Sorption of P in the soil-fill column decreased with increased STE and SFE application (reductions ranged from 99.1 to 74.4%). Results from this study indicate that there is potential for renovating wastewater in OSWTDS in selected soil-fill areas in reclaimed minelands.

title: Development, present state and future prospects of continuous combined cross-pit dumping in surface mining

authors: Drebenstedt C.

abstract: The most favourable variant of overburden removal in opencast mining is direct dumping of the overburden without the use of haulage means and by the shortest route over the raw material and onto the open floor. Cross-pit dumping combinations, each consisting of a continuously excavating and dumping machine with interconnected operation, have been used for the past 100 years for this economical variant of overburden removal. After first having been applied in Germany, this technique and technology began to used worldwide in the late 1950s. Since then, bucket wheel excavator and spreader combinations in particular, which nowadays achieve a cutting height of up to 30 m and a yearly output of 20 Mm<sup>3</sup>, are used effectively as a rule in the lower overburden section or to remove intermediate rock. As far as an extension of the scope of oreration of cross-pit dumping combinations is concerned, there are a number of technical and technological solutions available which make an effective exploitation of small or geologically complex deposits possible.

title: Optimizing short-term production schedules in surface mining: Integrating mine modeling software with AMPL/CPLEX
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Smith M.L.
abstract: Short-term production scheduling is the operational basis for mine production over time spans of days, weeks and months. Short-term schedules concentrate on making long-term mine plans operationally feasible and ensuring a steady flow of product for both meeting gross production targets and blending ore. Mathematical programming techniques have been applied to optimize short- and long-term production schedules, but widespread application of these techniques has been limited by the use of routines that are opaque to the end user or difficult to implement. Several examples are provided to illustrate the advantages of using the math modeling language AMPL in conjunction with Techbase, a popular mine modeling package. The strengths of MIP methods as applied to production scheduling are discussed, as are techniques for coping with the limitations of these algorithms.

title: Effect of particle size on the flocculation behaviour of ultra-fine clays in salt solutions
authors: Kotlyar L.S.; Sparks B.D.; LePage Y.; Woods J.R.
abstract: The Athabasca oil sands deposit in Alberta contains ∼5 × 10<sup>9</sup> m<sup>3</sup> of bitumen accessible by surface mining. During bitumen separation from the mined ore, ultra-fine (<300 nm) aluminosilicale clays only a few layers thick (U/F) are mobilized and become dispersed in the process water. In this water containing dissolved salts from natural deposits, U/F are capable of forming thixotropic gels. The consequence of this is the production of large volumes of mature fine tailings (MFT) with a high water holding capacity. For mine planning purposes, the objective of predicting and possibly mitigating MFT formation requires an understanding of the colloidal behaviour of U/F particles in salt solutions. In this work, photon correlation spcctroscopy and the deuterium NMR method are used to provide an insight into the U/F floc formation process. These results are correlated with conventional analysis of settling data.

title: An integrated approach to the design and management of surface mine haul roads in South Africa
authors: Thompson R.; Visser A.
operational_signals: agua_polvo_infraestructura; caminos_pisos_frentes; camion_extraccion; carguio_transporte; diseno_planificacion; haul road; haulage; mantenimiento_confiabilidad; mantenimiento_equipos; planificacion_diseno; transporte_acarreo
abstract: The surface mining and quarrying industry make extensive use of haul roads for bulk handling and transport of both ore and waste. Most of these haul road designs are based on local experience, and researchers at the University of Pretoria Departments of Civil and Mining Engineering recognised scope for improvement in design, construction and maintenance management guidelines for mine haul roads. Following four years of research, the application of these new and comprehensive guidelines has enabled mine operators in the Republic of South Africa to reduce total haulage costs significantly whilst providing optimally safe transport operating conditions. The worldwide expansion of surface mining has led to the development of very large off-highway trucks currently capable of hauling payloads in excess of 160 t. Typical axle loads ranging from 110 t to 170 t are applied to haul roads that have been, at best, empirically designed on the premise of "satisfactory" or "failed", both in terms of structure and function of the road. The use of these empirical pavement design techniques will prove inadequate when high axle loads are encountered. Not only will the maintenance costs of existing haul roads of inadequate thickness increase, but vehicle operating and maintenance costs will also increase prohibitively. Under these conditions there is thus a clearly defined need for improved technologies encompassing the construction and management techniques of flexible mine haul roads, appropriate for the wheel loads of vehicles now in use. The aim of this paper is to present the improved haul road design and management techniques which have been developed specifically for bulk material transport operations on South African surface mines. The paper illustrates how these developments are combined into an integrated design strategy combining mine layout, construction techniques, available material and road maintenance equipment with hauler choice to realise a reduction in haulage and road maintenance costs. In conclusion, it was found that the proposed mechanistic structural design methodology can significantly reduce road construction costs and improve the structural strength of the pavement. The improved functionality of a pavement was achieved through the specification of performance related wearing course material selection parameters, based on road-user acceptability criteria. Finally, the maintenance management design was centred on the development of a maintenance scheduling model from which it was seen that considerable financial benefit could accrue from applying a maintenance management system to mine haul roads.

title: Advantageous use of long-distance exploration in surface mining as exemplified by the Lusatian brown coal mining industry
authors: Drebenstedt C.; Knorr F.; Marek K.
abstract: Brown coal mining encroaches on the immediate environment like no other process of human activity. It is characteristic of the mining process in particular that it has an effect on nature over a large area and also over a long period of time. In order to lessen and compensate the effects of this encroachment by the mining industry, measures are adopted already during the mining process which aim, above all, to reduce the effects resulting from changed ground-water conditions and to ensure the creation of local abiotic features on the dumps and tips so that stable natural conditions can be established again after the cessation of mining operations. Long-distance exploration is a valuable aid for determining and recording the manifold and complicated relationships between mining and the environment. In this way the geometry and characteristic features of the objects in question can be determined. From sequential photographs showing changes in nature conclusions can be drawn, for instance, as to whether such changes have been caused by mining, as to the extent to which safety and preservation measures are effective, and whether recultivation can be carried out systematically. Together with other data on the area in question, long-distance exploration data can be stored in geo-information systems and can be evaluated and used very effectively for planning and monitoring purposes.

title: Different types of belt conveyors and their applications in surface mines
authors: Kesimal A.
abstract: Due to its nature, open-cast mining requires a variety of conveying systems able to offer: high capacity to suit the mine's throughput, flexibility by means of extensible or shiftable machines, to accommodate a continuously moving quarry-face, uphill conveying at steep angles in order to adapt to the mine grades, downhill conveying, accommodation of a variety of material sizes, and suitability for long hauls over difficult terrain. Most of the transportation studies related to surface mining will evaluate the economics of the belt conveying technology versus truck hauling. Sometimes, depending on specific local conditions, railway based transport will be considered. As conveyor technology advances and the operators increasingly take a long-term approach, flexible and reliable belt conveying systems become the method of choice in such operations. In this paper, presently and commonly used belt conveyors in surface mining have been reviewed.

title: An overview of diesel particulate exposures and control technology in the u.S. mining industry
authors: Haney R.A.; Saseen G.P.; Waytulonis R.W.
abstract: Studies of diesel particulate exposures in the U.S. mining industry indicate that diesel particulate exposures in surface mining operations are generally less than 0.2 mg/m<sup>3</sup>. Average diesel particulate exposures in underground coal mines using diesel-powered equipment ranged from 0.1 to 2.1 mg/m3. Average diesel particulate exposures in underground metal and nonmetal mines ranged from 0.3 to 1.6 mg/m<sup>3</sup>. The purpose of this article is to provide an overview on worker exposure to diesel particulate matter (DPM) and to discuss the effect of control technology on that exposure. Worker exposure has been assessed from in-mine diesel particulate measurements. The effect of control technology has been evaluated by a systems approach, which includes engine emission rate, mine ventilation system, and the effectiveness of engine after treatment devices. Studies conducted by the Mine Safety and Health Administration and the Bureau of Mines show that the primary means currently employed by the mining industry to control worker exposure to DPM include mine design, ventilation, engine maintenance, and the use of low sulfur fuel. Additional reductions in exposure can be obtained through the use of electronic engine technology. Commercially available after treatment devices are capable of reducing DPM by 25 to 95 percent. Reductions in exposure to DPM are dependent on the application of available engine emission control technology and modifications to mine ventilation systems. © 1997, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. title: An introduction to the integrated design of surface mine haul roads
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Thompson R.; Visser A.
operational_signals: agua_polvo_infraestructura; caminos_pisos_frentes; camion_extraccion; carguio_transporte; diseno_planificacion; haul road; haulage; mantenimiento_confiabilidad; transporte_acarreo
abstract: The world-wide expansion of surface mining has led to the development of very large off-highway trucks currently capable of hauling payloads in excess of 160t. Typical axle loads ranging from 110t to 170t are applied to haul roads that have been, at best, empirically designed on the premise of "satisfactory" or "failed", both in terms of structure and function of the road. The use of these empirical pavement design techniques will prove inadequate when high axle loads are encountered. Not only will the maintenance costs of existing haul roads of inadequate thickness increase, but vehicle operating and maintenance costs will also increase prohibitively. Under these conditions there is thus a clearly defined need for improved construction and management techniques for flexible mine haul roads, appropriate for the wheel loads of vehicles now in use. The aim of this paper is to introduce developments in haul road structural, functional and maintenance design and management which overcome the limitations associated with the previously empirical design techniques and to show how these developments are combined into an integrated design strategy combining construction techniques, available material and road maintenance equipment with hauler choice to realise a reduction in haulage and road maintenance costs. Future contributions will enumerate on the fundamental haul road structural, functional and maintenance design and management research from which these developments originated.

title: Achieving effective telerobotic control of industrial equipment
authors: Hunter D.; Wells D.; Chrystall K.; Feighan P.
keywords: Automation | Surface mining | Telerobotic control | Telerobotic equipment
operational_signals: automatizacion_datos; automatizacion_seguridad; camion_extraccion; desempeno_operacional; mantenimiento_confiabilidad; seguridad
abstract: Equipment which may be remotely operated, has some degree of on-board intelligence, and which for periods of time may operate autonomously, is referred to as telerobotic. Recent advances in electronics, computers and hydraulic equipment have dramatically reduced the cost and simplified the process of converting standard industrial equipment to telerobotic control. The benefits of telerobotic equipment include improved safety by removing the operator from dangerous situations, reduced maintenance costs and increased productivity. This technology has been proven in various military, nuclear, and police applications. The surface mining industry has expressed an interest in automation and is characterized by a willingness to use remotely operated equipment, however, the majority of telerobotic equipment currently in use is experimental or prototypical. Potential applications of telerobotic equipment for surface mining include remote operation of equipment near dangerous highwalls and other unsafe areas, utilization of robotic trucks for routine hauling operations, and control of jointed equipment In addition, component technologies of telerobotic systems are relevant to various forms of condition monitoring, operator feedback systems, and vehicle positioning. Attention must now be directed toward resolving more complex problems associated with enhancing feedback to the operator, improving the man/machine interface, and ultimately, improving efficiency. Removal of the human operator from the work site introduces significant complications in replacing the sensory inputs that an operator normally uses to efficiently run his machinery. These can be difficult to define and even more difficult to replicate remotely and may include restrictions pertaining to vision, hearing, and touch. In cooperation with Defence Research Establishment Suffield and the Alberta Research Council, Robotech Industries Ltd. is pursuing the development of additional technologies to further enhance an operator's ability to control remote telerobotic equipment. These developments include a head-mounted display, additional control station displays and improvements to coordinated motion control software. Prototypes of these developments are expected to be completed and tested by the fourth quarter of 1997.

It also allows connection to onboard PLCs (programmable logic controllers) supplied by major equipment manufacturers for monitoring machine data and global positioning systems (GPS). The DISPATCH mine management system has developed into the cornerstone of these operations. Every ton dug and every second worked is counted. Each equipment work assignment is optimized. A good example of this agreement is between Tamrock and Olympic Dam. Both parties benefit greatly from the agreement. Olympic Dam report that it saves money in equipment maintenance and parts and benefited from increased machine availability and reliability. Tamrock safeguards its parts sales from 'pirates' and generates more business with the Olympic Dam, while both parties able to benefit from product development in a very high productivity underground operation.

abstract: At Smoky River Coal Limited (SRCL), economic occurrences of structurally thickened coal deposits form attractive surface mining targets. title: State-of-the-art in mountaintop removal and contour mining
authors: White M.; Barata F.
abstract: Contour mining results in low mining ratios, but also lengthy outcrop disturbances (highwalls) and numerous environmental problems. Initially, the mining ratio in a contour mine operation was less than 7 to 1. Under present regulations and coal prices, contour mining has been reduced in the US. However, it is efficient in mountaintop removal operations. Contour mining incorporated into a mountaintop removal operation helps control drainage, minimize downslope placements (overshots) and balance the mining ratios. While mountaintop removal optimizes the coal reserve, the nature of this method results in coal being produced with higher mining ratios. This is due to the topography of the mining area. However, another contributor to these ratio increases include previous mining operations in the area. The mountaintop removal method of surface mining on this reserve began during the 1970s. The top of the mountain is removed to uncover the most economically minable coal seams. The overburden and interburden removed are placed in valley fills and backstacked on previously mined areas as required to produce the coal. Under ideal conditions, it is possible to extract nearly 100% of the minable coal, except for the outcrop barriers. -from Authors

title: Estimation of mercury content in tailings of the gold mine area of Poconé, Mato Grosso, Brazil
authors: von Tümpling W.; Zeilhofer P.; Ammer U.; Einax J.; Wilken R.D.
keywords: contamination through gold mining operations | Gold mine | Landsat satellite data | mercury content in tailings
abstract: As in many other parts of the world, gold is produced in the surface mining region of Poconé, Mato Grosso, Brazil, using mercury. The goal of this investigation was to estimate the amount of mercury in certain tailings and to determine the area of the land that has been contaminated by the gold mining operations. Mercury concentrations from 2 to 495 ng/g (dw) were determined in the tailing materials. It was observed that only isolated sites were acting as central points of contamination. Using digital Landsat satellite data (The-matic Mapper) and aerial photos, the sites degraded by the mining were classified, and their total area was estimated to be 12.3 km<sup>2</sup> in the region of Poconé. It was estimated, that 4.9 km<sup>2</sup> were occupied by the contaminated tailings. The mean height of the pile slags was determined to be 4.5 m. From the experimentally calculated average density of the material in the tailings, 2.01 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, the total mercury content in the piles of tailings was estimated to be 1600 ± 350 kg. © 1995, Ecomed Publishers. title: Mining equipment into the 21st century
authors: Wiebmer J.
abstract: Several industry trends are putting new demands on surface mining equipment. This is true both on the 'hard' side of the equipment business - the research and product development programs, and on the 'soft' side - the business processes, human resources and competitive strategies. This article describes seven key industry trends and the impact each is having on surface mining equipment suppliers. These trends are, respectively, globalization, consolidation, improved asset management and utilization, a scarcity of skilled labor, environmental issues, cost competition, and information management.

title: Continous surface mining equipment: how to achieve success
authors: Delilla E.

abstract: Continuous mining systems (bucketwheel excavators or continuous mining machines by Wirtgen, Voest-Alpine, etc.) must be matched to specific operating conditions. There are no "off-the-shelf' machines, and there are usually no simple modifications that will make a machine perform differently in response to changing mining conditions. In some cases, it has taken years for a mismatched machine to be made to perform effectively. There have been numerous cases where the machines were just not compatible with the conditions and never performed to expectations. Continuous mining systems can work. They offer an opportunity for high productivity at low operating costs for mining operations. However, everyone involved must be aware of the many tasks that must be successfully completed to apply these systems in their mines. -Author

title: Arch of Illinois - look to the future
authors: Bierei G.
abstract: The application of a more appropriate technology puts Arch of Illinois at the region's most profitable position as the mining complex undergoes a gradual shift from surface mining to underground mining. In response to dwindling low ratio reserves and increasing land acquisition and environmental costs, the mining complex shifted its attention to underground reserves. This entailed a corresponding change from truck haulage to beltline haulage. The underground operations brought about an increase in the amount of coal fines and this involved the construction of a fine coal circuit that would recover particles down to -150 μm (-100 mesh). Meanwhile, to maintain the profitability of remaining surface reserves, Arch of Illinois uses modified continuous miners and a battery haulage.

title: On-highway truck engine tackles mining applications
authors: Wadman B.
abstract: While engine emissions are a concern in virtually all equipment markets these days, nowhere are they more critical than in mining applications. Facing these constraints, manufacturers of mining equipment have been particularly interested in the continuing development of electronically controlled diesel engines. In dealing with the emissions question, the Wagner Mining and Construction Equipment Co. of Portland, OR, has turned to an on-highway truck engine, the electronically controlled Detroit Diesel series 60 diesel. Wagner is using the engine in both its underground and surface mining equipment and is among the first manufacturers to use the series 60 engine in a non-road application other than marine. The electronic control and diagnostic capabilities of the series 60 engine provide improved reliability in hostile underground environments. In addition, the electronic control system keeps the engine in tune without the frequent adjustments needed with mechanical control systems.

title: From coercion to partnership in federal partial preemption: SMCRA, RCRA, and OSH act
authors: Scicchitano M.J.; Hedge D.M.
abstract: This article examines the experiences of three important partial-preemption programs-the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 (SMCRA), the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 (OSH Act), and the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act of 1976 (RCRA)-over the last two decades to improve our understanding of how federal-state interactions have shaped the regulatory partnership. The evidence we gather suggests that the control of regulatory programs has shifted over time back and forth between the federal government and the states. In the initial years of these programs, what the Congress intended to be a regulatory partnership was, in effect, almost total federal preemption of state authority. Under the Ronald Reagan administration, the opposite occurred; federal regulation in many cases became de facto state regulation as federal officials essentially abdicated their oversight responsibility. By the end of the 1980s, the federal government began again to assert greater control over intergovernmental regulatory programs. The regulatory relationship that emerged is one in which the federal government and the states share responsibility and authority for the implementation of these programs. © 1993, CSF Associates.

title: Grouting of old flooded workings at M. Mayerova Mine in Czechoslovakia
authors: Kipko E.J.; Spichak Y.N.; Polozov Y.A.; Kipko A.E.; Hepnar P.
abstract: The paper is concerned with the design of a surface mining operation above a waterlogged underground mine workings in order to prevent ingress of water and control mine water pollution. The site of investigation was situated at M. Mayerova Mine, near the city of Karlovy Vary, Western Czechoslovakia which was operational at the end of 19th century. These mine workings were abandoned and subsequently, presented the a problem of eliminating flooded mine workings encountered in Jozef Seam at a depth of 176 m and two 4 m. diameter, No. 2 and No. 5, vertical mine shafts. The proposed mining operations were planned to extract overlying Antonin Seam at a depth of 88 m. below the surface by open casting technique and to prevent ingress of water into the planned workings. This problem had been complicated by a hydraulic connection of flooded workings of the Jozef Seam, recharged from the intersected fault zone, with regional reserves of mineral thermal springs of the city of Karlovy Vary through fissured sandstones and quartzites underlying the coal layer. For resolving the problem and in accordance with the project report and methodology of Integrated Grouting Technique of P/A Spetstamponazhgeologia (STG), Geoindustria Enterprise, Czechoslovakia has conducted injection of the designed volume of clay-cement grout into the flooded workings. The grout was pumped through surface drilled boreholes under specified regimes. As a result, the inflow to the Jozef seam workings was reduced from 0.5 m<sup>3</sup>/min to 0.0002 m<sup>3</sup>/min, ground water temperature fell down from 31°C to 18°C. The paper deals with the actual data of this original project. © 1993 Springer-Verlag.

title: Dynamic elasticity and strength anisotropy of some surficial rocks
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Inyang H.I.; Fish K.
abstract: Rock mass classification systems that comprise both rock material properties and large-scale discontinuities are essential in surface mining operations, tunneling and rock foundation engineering. As reported in this paper, point load strength measurements made on limestone, sandstone, granite, basalt and syenite rock samples indicate anisotropy ratios (axial to diametral) ranging approximately from 2.0 to 9.5. In general, direct proportionality exists between measured strength values in the two orthogonal directions. Furthermore, axial and diametral strength values are respectively, directly proportional to the dynamic elastic modulus of the samples. Values for the latter were obtained indirectly through density and sonic wave transit time measurements. Although it is known to be significant in rock excavation processes, rock quality designation (RQD) exhibits no discernible relationship with elastic modulus or point load strength of each of the rock samples tested. Along with the results of previous investigations, experimental data obtained in this investigation are used to discuss the utility of combining rock material strength measures and information on the distribution of joints (beyond the scale of small test samples) to characterize rock masses. © 1992, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. title: Control of surface mine drainage at Coeur d'Alene's thunder mountain mine
authors: Mohr R.
operational_signals: agua_polvo_infraestructura; desague_drenaje; diseno_planificacion; mine drainage; operacion_general; planificacion_diseno
abstract: Practical applications to sediment control can be applied to surface mining operations in a cost-effective manner. The key to establishing a functional water management and reclamation program is to begin with a thorough understanding of the hydrologic regime of the project area. Once the hydrologic design parameters set, the next step is to divide the drainage areas within the project area of disturbance into individual subdrainages. The intent here is to minimize the total flow that can be generated from any one area to a level that will not cause erosion of native soils. By dispersing runoff into small components, non-point source impacts from surface runoff can be minimized. Once an effective water management plan has been established, the program can be modified annually over the life of the mine.

title: Applying knowledge-based expert systems to provide guidance for the safe storage of coal
authors: Ren T.; Denby B.; Singh R.
abstract: The application of a prototype knowledge-based expert system for spontaneous heating, essh, in surface coal stockpiling operations is described. A brief review of earlier studies concerning the assessment of self-heating risk in stockpiles is presented. Based upon extensive analyses of the incidents of coal storage problems with spontaneous heating, the paper identifies the significant contributory factors which may have caused them. The stacking and precautionary techniques, or the rules of thumb, accumulated from years of experience and research, with particular reference to the safe storage of coal, are also discussed. This high level knowledge is further refined and consolidated into a knowledge-based expert system which aims to replicate the reasoning of human experts in reaching a decision. The system assesses the spontaneous combustion risk by using certainty factor techniques. It is capable of identifying common faults and recommending systematic procedures and methods for inexperienced engineers in handling stockpiles being planned, under construction and in use. Future development of the current system in surface mining operations is highlighted. The approach outlined in this paper offers a new managerial technique and shows how the incidents of spontaneous heating, weathering of coal and environmental impact can be minimized or avoided entirely through appropriate storage and handling, by applying an expert system approach. © 1991 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V.

abstract: As the nature of coal mining changes in Australia and thin seams are exposed after years of overburden removal by draglines, a need has arisen for a machine that gets the paydirt on its way to the stockpiles as quickly and cost effectively as possible. Surface miners are being seen as the best available machine for this purpose because they are continuous and they integrate a number of mining processes. They do away with the need for blasting, ripping, scraping, and primary crushing. There are three suppliers of surface miners in Australia: Tutts, Wirtgen and Krupp Australia. Another advantage of the surface miner is that it can be used to mine selectively and get the best use of labour and capital investment in the machinery. This paper describes the different surface miners.

title: Natural Recovery of Microbial Populations in Mixed Overburden Surface-Mine Spoils of Texas
authors: Mott J.B.; Zuberer D.A.
keywords: Coal | Lignite | Microorganisms | Overburden | Spoil | Strip mining | Surface mining
abstract: The chemical and physical properties of mixed overburden (spoil) from lignite surface mining operations in the southern United States have been well documented. However, there is little information on the microbiological characteristics of these spoils. To investigate the impact of the mining process on soil microbial populations, we determined the abundance of various microbial groups, including several involved in nitrogen (N) transformations, in variously aged spoils (1-10 years postmining) of east Texas. Numbers of aerobic, heterotrophic bacteria, actinomycetes, and fungi in fresh spoil were lower than those in an unmined soil but returned to premining (unmined control) levels within 1.5 years in revegetated spoils. Algal numbers had not reached pre-mining levels within 10 years after mining. Numbers of fungal and algal species were low in more recently disturbed soils. Numbers of N<inf>2</inf>-fixing cyanobacteria were lower in most soils, but free-living N<inf>2</inf>-fixing bacteria were abundant in both fresh and older spoils. Nitrifying bacteria were more abundant in spoil and numbers tended to be greater at the older sites than in the unmined soil. All microbial populations were markedly diminished at an acidic area (pH 2.8-3.0) in the 10-year site. Microbial populations in recently leveled spoil did not decline with depth down to 90 cm. Results from this study suggest a relatively rapid natural restoration of microbial populations in revegetated, mixed overburden although there were indications of declines in species richness in some groups. Bacteria meditating the major transformations of N were present at all stages of the reclamation process. © 1991 Taylor & Francis.

abstract: A world-scale surface mining operation is associated with the Syncrude Oilsands Plant. title: Evaluation of Aquifer Behavior and Characteristics in the Singrauli Coalfield, Central India
authors: Choubey V.; Shankaranarayana I.
abstract: Hydrological investigations were conducted to determine the aquifer characteristics, recharge boundary location, and the amount of ground water which can be withdrawn safely in order to minimize potential ground–water contamination from open pit coal mining. The results of the pumping tests indicated that a recharge boundary is located at a distance of 163 m. The recharge boundary was determined to be a stream trending N–S and situated at about 200 meters from the pumping well, closely corroborating the field situation with pump test data. From these studies it is concluded that water–supply wells should be completed in the confined aquifer. The impact of surface mining of coal on the ground–water system in Singrauli Coalfield, Central India has been investigated. Surface–water and hydrogeologic analyses were conducted in Jayant block. Field studies measured the infiltration characteristics of surface‐mined land, determined surface–water runoff, and analyzed the hydrogeologic impacts of surface mining. This study provides the framework for three–dimensional analysis of such problems as the hydrogeology, risk of potential contamination, mine flooding, highwall stability, and reclaimed land surface. title: Redundancy works well in blasting
authors: Chironis N.
abstract: In surface mining where blasting is generally employed, every so often a blast goes off imperfectly, with some holes being cut off and misfired. Such a situation leaves powder in the muck and many loaded holes to shoot again, with the overburden either poorly fragmented or poorly cast, depending on the design. Atlas Powder Co., Dallas, Tex., has a nonelectric blast initiation system that assures there is more than one initiation path to each blasthole to avoid misfirings and shutdowns. Called the Blastmaster Redundant Trunkline Delay (RTD), the system has been developed for use in surface mines and quarries where more than one row of holes is detonated in delayed sequence in a blast. Drummond Coal Co., Jasper, Ala., was the first large-scale surface coal mining company to apply the concept of redundancy to its nonelectric blast initiation systems.

title: Pre-splitting with the new AIRDEK technique
authors: Bussey J.; Borg D.
abstract: AIRDEK pre-splitting is a new and affordable blasting technique for high-wall and perimeter control in surface mining. It differs from conventional pre-splitting in that a specific quantity of explosives is loaded in the bottom of the hole and a large part of the blast hole (except for stemming) remains empty at the time of firing. Extensive field testing has proved that the AIRDEK method is significantly more economical than other methods. The key component in AIRDEK deck pre-splitting is the 'Power Plug', a simple inflatable device. Because AIRDEK pre-splitting permits higher standing highwalls, there is a better utilization of coal reserves which could not be mined with lower walls.

title: Mathematical modelling for estimation of minewater inflow to a surface mining operation
authors: Singh R.; Reed S.

abstract: Estimation of water inflow to a surface mining operation is a necessary requirement for mine drainage design. The water in a shallow surface mine may originate solely from a surface source and from the atmosphere in the form of precipitation. Water in deep mining excavations below the groundwater table may originate from a surface source or as atmospheric precipitation as well as from the groundwater system. Inflow of surface water to a mining excavation can be predicted by hydrological balance investigation of a mining catchment. The paper briefly describes the hydrological cycle of a mining catchment together with the technique of estimating inflow from a surface source. The groundwater inflow to a mining excavation is mainly a consequence of the interaction of groundwater system, hydrogeological characteristics of the rock mass and the mining geometry. The water inflow regime is determined by the incision of one or more aquifers by the mining excavation and the relative hydrogeological characteristics of the various aquifers. The paper identifies various possible flow regimes in the vicinity of mining excavation. The groundwater inflow can be estimated by one of the following techniques:- Equivalent flow approach - Two-dimensional flow equations - Numerical techniques incorporating the Finite Element Method, Finite Difference Method or the Boundary Element Method. © 1988 Springer-Verlag.

title: OVERBURDEN SPREADERS-LAYOUT CRITERIA AS FUNCTION OF OPERATIONAL CONDITIONS.
authors: Benecke K.J.
abstract: In surface mining, waste handling systems with continuous operation mode are composed of different handling devices. They form a chain with the spreader (stacker) as the final link. The paper deals with the dependence of spreader design and operational conditions. A spreader places waste in final location in high and deep dumps. The overall dump height decides the spreader geometry. This refers to both the receiving and discharge conveyor length. Stability and inclination of the dump slopes play a part, too. Handling rate and mobility are further design criteria. Crawlers are today's standard for the main undercarriage, best suited to poor traction conditions and bearing capacity prevailing on dumped waste. Tripper car and feeding conveyor support are subjected to operation mode, mobility and handling rate in their design, too.

title: COMPUTER-ASSISTED MINE PRODUCTION PLANNING.
authors: Hendry J.W.
abstract: This paper will discuss the application of tools and the evolution of computer-assisted procedures in the production planning process at Quintette Coal Limited (QCL). In 1986 QLC produced 5. 3 Mt of clean coal from their surface mining operation located in northern British Columbia. The structural complexity of the sedimentary deposit and high rate of mining necessitate the consideration of large amounts of geological information which continually updates the interpretation. There are multiple unit operations required during the process of mining through a given multi-seam sequence, which results in many interdependent faces, and multiple iterations of scheduling sequences in order to satisfy a given set of objectives. In order to facilitate these activities in a timely fashion, it was recognized that a computer systems' capability needed to be developed which could increase the efficiency of information input, manipulation and output.

title: Oil sands tailings sludge solidification and bitumen recovery
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Joshi R.C.; Prasad B.D.
abstract: Canada is a forerunner in the development of oil sands mining and processing technology. At present two commercial plants, both of them surface mining operations are producing approximately 200,000 of syncrude per day. At both of these plants a hot water separation process is used. The vast amounts of tailings, consisting of bitumen, sand, fines and water, generated from the hot water extraction process while recovering bitumen during surface mining operation, must be stored within gigantic man-made reservoirs created by constructing high dykes or dams. In this study, the potential of lime addition for stabilization of the sludge and recovery of bitumen has been investigated. Results of study indicate that more than 50 percent water as well as the bitumen can be recovered from sludge by centrifuging alone. With lapse of time, lime addition causes solidification of sludge as reflected by strength increase of treated and mompacted sludge. The implication of this investigation is that bitumen recovery from sludge is possible with the possibility of direct feed to the upgrading plant. The process discussed in this paper is economically measible. This is particularly true in those areas where bitumen recovery by surface mining is relatively high due to a high waste/ore ratio and when quality of mined oil sands is relatively low. © 1988, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

abstract: The paper discusses the use of high speed, side-slewable belt conveyors in large-scale surface mining, in conjunction with in-pit crushing. The reasons for the use of such a transport system are discussed and compared to other systems. Bucket Chain Excavators (BCE), or Bucket Wheel Excavators (BWE) used in surface mining can only be fully utilised with a continuous transport system, such as a conveyor belt. Loading of the belts is carried out by the excavators in the pit and the spoil is taken around the pit to the spoil bank. In cases where the overburden is thick and competent, pre-stripping and crushing are required, to enable the use of belt conveyors for transport. The application criteria and the method of use of such systems are described, and economical factors are considered. © 1988 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V.

abstract: High-volume surface mining operations such as the Canadian oil sands mines depend on high-capacity equipment for excavation and transportation of overburden and ore. Dragline and bucket wheel excavator/conveyor systems have been developed to high levels of productivity, and numerous improvements have been made in all phases of mining practice. However, mines throughout the world continue to devote considerable effort to developing innovative new technologies, operating techniques, and procedures for improving productivity. Operators of such mines should periodically prepare an awareness report, evaluating outside technology for in-house use. This type of intelligence and technology transfer is vital to maintenance of competitive and cost effective operations. This article briefly reviews some technology and operating practices that have recently become available to large-scale surface mines.

title: Blasting in overburden with site mixed slurry - a techno-economic assessment

abstract: The future years of Indian coal mining will see a significant increase in the production of coal from large mechanized opencast mines and huge quantities of overburden removal by deploying large capacity dragline and other heavy earth moving machinery. To attain overall economics, the very initial operating such as blasting, has to be very much cost efective as well as low manpower intensive. This can be achieved only by bulk handling of explosives and more R&D efforts to generate direct cost reduction in addition to the highest degree of safety. This article highlights investment, annual production capacity, average stripping ratio and the total excavation of overburden of some of the major ongoing surface mining projects in the coal sector of India. Various technical and economical benefits associated with mechanized bulk handling of site-mixed explosive slurries are reviewed.

title: MODERN EQUIPMENT FOR KENNECOTT'S BINGHAM CANYON COPPER MINE.
authors: Kaerst D.
abstract: In order to maintain and/or increase in the economic viability of their companies, mining operators are therefore being forced to adopt rationalization programs, particularly in high-wage-level countries. In the surface mining industry, particularly as far as hard rock mining is concerned, such ratonalization measures generally signify a transition from purely discontinuously functioning extraction and conveying equipment to continuously operating equipment or to a combination of these two modes. An up-to-date project is illustrated in this article. title: Determinants of chronic bronchitis and lung dysfunction in Western Australian gold miners
authors: Holman C.D.J.; Psaila-Savona P.; Roberts M.; McNulty J.C.
abstract: The relation of chronic bronchitis and respiratory dysfunction to age, tobacco smoking, and occupational exposure to surface and underground mining operations were examined in a cross sectional survey of 1363 men employed in the Kalgoorlie mining industry in 1985. Overall, the prevalence of chronic bronchitis was 14%. Eleven per cent of the workers had obstructive lung disorder (FEV<inf>1</inf>/FVC < 0.70) and 9% had restrictive lung disorder (FVC < 0.80 of predicted for height and age). There was little change in the prevalence of chronic bronchitis from that observed in a survey of the same industry in 1961-2. Only 1% of the workers in 1985 had radiographic signs of silicosis compared with 22% in 1961-2. Age, smoking, and underground mining experience all exerted strong effects on the development of chronic bronchitis with or without associated respiratory function abnormalities. After control of confounding by age and smoking, it was estimated that compared with a lifetime non-miner, the odds ratio (OR) of chronic bronchitis was 1.8 (95% confidence interval, 1.0-3.3) for one to nine years underground mining gold, 2.5 (1.2-5.2) for 10-19 years, and 5.1 (2.4-10.9) for 20 or more years. Underground mining of minerals other than gold was also associated with chronic bronchitis (OR = 5.1; 95% CI, 1.1-25.0) whereas exclusive surface mining had only a small empirical effect (OR = 1.3; 95% CI, 0.6-2.5). It is estimated that the proportion of cases of chronic bronchitis in working underground miners due to occupational factors is 50%. The results support the existence of an industrial cause of chronic bronchitis, although caution must be exercised in generalising the results to miners with progressive and severe respiratory impairment.

title: LOW-FREQUENCY VIBRATIONS PRODUCED BY SURFACE MINE BLASTING OVER ABANDONED UNDERGROUND MINES.
source: Report of Investigations United States Bureau of Mines
authors: Siskind D.; Stachura V.; Nutting M.
abstract: Bureau of Mines researchers assisted the U. S. Office of Surface Mining (OSM) by studying complaint-producing blasting vibrations resulting from an active surface mine operating over abandoned mine workings beneath the surface mine and the nearby town of Blanford, IN. Ground vibrations were of high amplitude and dominated by unusual and more structure response-producing low frequencies (4-8 Hz) than previous studies at other sites. These conditions resulted primarily from the geologic structure as the vibration propagating medium. Blast designs were partly responsible, with high level casting and complex multidelayed blasts producing wave interaction and constructive reinforcement. The traditional 8-ms criteria for separating charge weights per delay appears insufficient for this low-frequency site.

title: AUTOMATION, SIMPLIFICATION OF OPERATION AND INCREASE IN PERFORMANCE OF SELF-PROPELLED CONSTRUCTION AND SURFACE MINING MACHINES BY USE OF ELECTRONICS.
source: Transactions of the Iron and Steel Institute of Japan
authors: Leidinger G.
abstract: The complexities of surface mining and construction machines have reached a degree at which operators are no longer in a position to operate them continuously in the most efficient way and guarantee full utilization of the available performance. It is necessary, therefore, to ease the operation, either by supplying the operator with information on the overall status of his machine or by giving him direct operating instructions. This information must be presented to the operator in such a manner that it requires only a small amount of attention. By the introduction of closed control circuits the operator can be partly - or in some cases entirely - relieved from the direction of certain functions of the machine. Increased efficiency by reductions in fuel consumption and maintenance is also made possible by improved machine monitoring techniques. These rely on the application of microelectronics in connection with variable hydraulic systems. The main emphasis of automation today is on these means of optimizing the performance of the machine.

title: REDUCTION OF QUARRYING COST THROUGH USE OF CRUSHER/BELT CONVEYOR SYSTEMS.
authors: Mueller G.
abstract: In the 1950s the German cement industry was the first to develop crusher/belt conveyor systems. Handling rates of 250 tph and sizes of less than 50 mm did not present any problem for rubber belt conveyors. By 1975 conveyor installations capable of handling 1000 tph and by 1980 of 2000 tph were available. While the impetus to these development efforts emanated from the cement industry where limestone is the raw material, crusher/conveyor systems made their appearance in 1975 in the surface mining of bauxite and phosphate and, in 1980, copper ore. In 1986, Krupp Industrietechnik GmbH will supply the first 6000 tph mining system for iron ore. It will be commissioned in Australia. This article discusses mobile crushing plant markets, costs, and other aspects of the subject.

title: Nickel, cadmium, and selenium levels in native soil, overburden, and spoil materials
authors: Pitt J.; Hossner L.; Melton J.
abstract: Nickel (Ni), cadmium (Cd), and selenium (Se) analyses showed that there was no significant difference in the concentration of these elements when compared over the three sample types examined (native soil, overburden, and spoil materials obtained from four surface mining operations in Texas). The soils belong to the Paleustalf, Paleudult, Hapludalf, and Paleudalf Great Groups. Ranges in total concentrations of the individual elements were 4.01 to 71.4 mg kg<sup>-1</sup> Ni, 0.00 to 2.46 mg kg<sup>-1</sup> Cd, and 0.04 to 10.7 mg kg<sup>-1</sup> Se for the native soil, overburden, and spoil samples. At each site, the geological environments of deposition had significantly different levels of Ni, Cd, and Se. Depositional environments containing higher concentrations of fine materials (Backswamp, flood basin, etc.) had the highest concentrations of Ni and Cd. Selenium was highest in the lignite and deposits closely associated with the lignite. Results of this study indicate that no significant elevation of total Ni, Cd, and Se would be expected from the complete mixing of overburden following the surface mining operation.

title: EVALUATING WHEEL LOADERS AND FRONT SHOVELS.
authors: Anon
abstract: The availability of hydraulic front shovels in the 10- to 12-yd**3 class increases the number of large loading machines for surface mining. Although both the wheel loader and front shovel have distinct advantages, and each can often handle the work of the other, the economics are different. Manufacturers of front shovels often claim their machines are a better choice in tough digging applications because of high breakout forces and faster cycle times. Although the hydraulic shovel cycled faster, the wheel loader had a significant advantage in the amount of overburden moved per bucket load. The result, the wheel loader uncovered 2700 st more coal per eight-hour shift - a 30% production advantage. Even when comparing a 13-yd**3 front shovel to a 13. 5-yd**3 wheel loader, which Caterpillar did in a more recent study, the advantage still goes to the wheel loader.

title: Dynamic programming with colour graphics smoothing for open-pit design on a personal computer
authors: Zhang S.; Starfield A.M.
keywords: dynamic programming | Open-pit mine design | surface mining
abstract: Dynamic programming is a technique which has been used to design the optimum final surface mining pit limit. In using dynamic programming there is a trade-off: if the geometric constraints are specified too strictly, the pit limit will not be the optimum, but if they are specified more loosely, then the computed pit contours must be smoothed. The smoothing process has usually been manual and is time consuming. In this paper a colour graphics computer routine is presented. title: Robots and mining: The implications for Australian industry in the 1980's
authors: Kassler M.
abstract: After elucidating the terms ‘mining’ and ‘robot’, a historical background to the problem of mining is described, with emphasis on the use of technology. Various reasons for the increasing utilisation of technology are discussed, as regards the mechanisation of existing operations and those unachievable without new technology. It is asserted that the mining industry has a number of particular features that make increasing mechanisation especially attractive. The point is made that the ultimate stage of the historical tendency towards the use of new technology is fully automatic mining, a goal that may not be realised, however, in the next decade. The above historical discussion is followed by a critical appraisal of the conservative nature of the Australian industry and the study of the various factors that contribute to the slow uptake of new technology in mining. Attention is then concentrated on the general problem of robots and mining. It is shown that worldwide there were no applications of robots to mining up to the end of 1981. A wide study has been carried out to identify some uses of robots in mining, but without success. The next topic to be discussed is the widespread confusion about robots and teleoperators. The fundamental difference between the two is underlined, and particular attention is paid to Thring's teleoperator mining concept (telechiric mining). It is emphasized that telechiric mining will have no significant impact upon Australian mining in this decade. These pessimistic asssessments are followed by claims that in some areas robotic concepts, though not robots themselves, could have a considerable effect on mining automation in the 1980's, both in Australia and elsewhere. The following projects are enumerated as possible candidates for applying robotic concepts: Surface mining; Mine development; Underground coal transport; Coal winning; Coal preparation. In order to make progress, it is recommended that a robotics expert ought to be included in the interdisciplinary teams studying the problem of mining automation. The last part of this paper is devoted to Australia's need for robotic mining. A list of systems involving robotic concepts is presented that may be realised in the current decade. It is maintained that Australia ought to develop a few of such systems for the domestic and international markets, and that the short-term needs of the Australian mining industry are fundamentally different from those of other Australian industries as regards robots. Hence, decisions regarding robots for mining should be made independently from those appertaining to automation problems of other industries. © 1985, Cambridge University Press. All rights reserved.

title: BLASTING AND BLASTING LIABILITIES.
authors: Ludwiczak J.
abstract: Blasting in surface coal mining has changed greatly over the last ten years. The main causes for these changes have been the new laws governing the use of explosives. These new laws have been developed so as not to cause problems to those who live around a mining or blasting site. Laws such as the Federal Surface Mining act of 1977 included new requirements governing not only the use of explosives but also the certification and training requirements for blasters. These laws and regulations were promulgated mainly for the benefit of those individuals who live close to blasting and mining operations.

source: Information Circular United States Bureau of Mines
authors: Long D.
abstract: An evaluation of hazards associated with getting on and off large surface mining vehicles showed that most of the accidents occur at the point where personnel attempt to mount or dismount the machine at ground level. This report describes the design and in-mine testing of improved access systems.

title: Control of groundwater in surface mining
authors: Brawner C.O.
operational_signals: desague_drenaje; diseno_planificacion; equipment maintenance; equipos_mantenimiento; mantenimiento_confiabilidad; mantenimiento_desempeno; mantenimiento_equipos; operacion_general; perforacion; perforacion_tronadura; pit drainage; planificacion_diseno; tronadura
abstract: The presence of groundwater in surface mining operations often creates serious problems. The most important is generally a reduction in stability of the pit slopes. This is caused by pore water pressures and hydrodynamic shock due to blasting which reduce the shear strength and seepage pressures, water in tension cracks and increased unit weight which increase the shear stress. Groundwater and seepage also increase the cost of pit drainage, shipping, drilling and blasting, tyre wear and equipment maintenance. Surface erosion may also be increased and, in northern climates, ice flows on the slopes may occur. Procedures have been developed in the field of soil mechanics and engineering of dams to obtain quantitative data on pore water pressures and rock permeability, to evaluate the influence of pore water and seepage pressures on stability and to estimate the magnitude of ground-water flow. Based on field investigations, a design can be prepared for the control of groundwater in the slope and in the pit. Methods of control include the use of horizontal drains, blasted toe drains, construction of adits or drainage tunnels and pumping from wells in or outside of the pit. Recent research indicates that subsurface drainage can be augmented by applying a vacuum or by selective blasting. Instrumentation should be installed to monitor the groundwater changes created by drainage. Typical case histories are described that indicate the approach used to evaluate groundwater conditions. © 1982 Springer-Verlag.

title: Watersheds in muskeg terrain. 2. Evaluations based on water chemistry
authors: Schwartz F.W.; Milne-Home W.A.
abstract: This paper discusses the application of data on stream water chemistry to regional groundwater evaluation, hydrograph separation, and evaluation of the effects of basin disturbance. We have selected for analysis the Firebag, Steepbank and Muskeg River basins, and Hartley and Thickwood Creek basins in northern Alberta, Canada. They cover slightly more than 9000 km<sup>2</sup> within a region containing vast quantities of surface mineable, oil sand deposits. All basins are drift covered and underlain by bedrock that can range in age from Precambrian to Cretaceous. Comparison of chemical data for stream water from all basins with that for groundwater from Hartley Creek basin confirms that groundwater is a major source of streamflow in winter. Indications are that this groundwater inflow is almost entirely from glacial drift. Hydrograph separations based on chemical parameters indicate that during the spring and summer the proportion of groundwater in the streamflow is less than winter values with the largest contribution by far coming from the drainage of muskeg. Muskeg thus exerts important control on stream discharge and chemistry. If surface mining in these basins causes the removal of muskeg and replacement by mineral soil, stream discharge from affected areas will be less during summer and more during spring runoff and stormflow periods. As well, major-ion concentrations should be generally higher in the summer and fall months. However, the impact of local disturbances in a larger basin will be diminished downstream as waters from affected areas are mixed with other waters. © 1982.

title: Hydrological problems of surface mining.
authors: Wood P.
abstract: Recent literature concerned with the physical problems arising from the interrelationships between hydrology ad the surface mining of coal is reviewed. title: The belchatow, Poland, earthquakes of 1979 and 1980 induced by surface mining
authors: Gibowicz S.; Droste Z.; Guterch B.; Hordejuk J.
abstract: Five seismic events occurred between August 1979 and May 1980 in the Belchatow trench area in central Poland, where large brown-coal deposits have been surface-mined since 1976. The three largest shocks had a local magnitude M<inf>L</inf> = 3.5, seismic moment M<inf>o</inf> = 1.5 · 10<sup>14</sup> N-m and source radius r = 350 m, approximately. The tremors had maximum intensity between 5 and 6, and from the magnitude-intensity-depth relation, the focal depth was estimated to be between 1 and 5 km. The Belchatow tremors are the manifestation of an unusual type of induced seismicity, i.e., seismicity connected with surface mining. The removal of overburden and extensive ground-water withdrawal by the mining operations seem to be direct factors responsible for stress concentration, although preexisting tectonic stress might be the most important indirect factor responsible for the origin of these events. © 1981.

title: Depositional setting and groundwater quality in coal-bearing sediments and spoils in western North Dakota ( USA).
source: Recent and Ancient Nonmarine Depositional Environments Models for Exploration
authors: Groenewold G.; Rehm B.; Cherry J.
abstract: Studies of several active and proposed surface coal-mining sites in western N Dakota have resulted in the development of a hydrogeochemical framework which accounts for the chemical characteristics of groundwater in coal-bearing strata. There is much regional similarity in the hydrogeochemical characteristics of shallow aquifers. SO<inf>4</inf> <sup>=</sup> and HCO<inf>3</inf> <sup>-</sup> are commonly dominant anions. Na and Ca are generally the dominant cations. The pH of the groundwater normally ranges from 7 to 9. Critical hydrogeochemical processes include pyrite oxidation, carbonate mineral dissolution, and sulfate reduction. During surface mining operations unweathered materials are commonly emplaced in the zone of active weathering. Hydrochemical data from postmining landscapes suggest that severe degradation of groundwater quality is possible in some settings. The degree of weathering, dissolution, and ion exchange is largely dependent upon mineralogical variables in the overburden sediments. Degradation of groundwater quality in postmining landscapes can be minimized if these factors are integrated within the framework of mine design. -from Author

title: DEVELOPMENT OF THE WABCO 353FT TWIN ENGINE ELEVATING SCRAPER.
authors: Hurst C.
abstract: The development of the WABCO 353FT Twin Engine Elevating Scraper for surface mining applications is an example of advancements being made in mining equipment technology. The 353FT optimizes the benefits of the various scraper configurations available by combining the ability to work under adverse conditions, due to its all-wheel drive, with large capcity and the self loading feature of an elevating scraper. Two Detroit Diesel 12V-71T, turbocharged engines drive identical Allison planetary powershift transmissions with variable-input-power torque converters and hydraulic retarders. The tractor engine, equipped with N75 injectors, is rated at 525 brake horsepower (391. 6 kW) at 2100 rpm. The scraper engine, with N70 injectors is rated at 500 brake horsepower (373. 0 kW). The 12V-71T is a 12-cylinder, two-stroke engine. The throttles of both engines are simultaneously controlled through the use of a single throttle pedal which operates two air throttle/cylinders. A second throttle pedal, which controls the tractor engine only, can be used when power from the scraper engine is not required, such as in tight turn situations. Traction sensing differentials automatically maintain torque to the wheels with the best traction. The scraper cutter is driven hydraulically, the elevator electrically.

The author cites the following problems which he claims will prevent this goal from being reached: 1. Clean Air Act of 1970, 2. Federal Mine Safety Act of 1969, 3. Federal Leasing Regulations, 4. Transportation Facilities, 5. Technical Manpower, 6. Mine Labor, 7. Equipment Availability. The United States is fortunate in having one of the world's largest reserves of coal. Total measured and indicated reserves of coal in beds over 28 inches thick and under less than 1000 feet of overburden totaled 434 billion tons as of January 1, 1974. Of these reserves, 297 billion tons were considered underground reserves and 137 billion tons capable of being mined by surface mining. But unless a commitment is made to coal by the Government which will remove the restrictions already in place and prevent other restrictions from being placed on the industry, this coal will not be mined, in the author's opinion.

title: FRONT SHOVEL WORKS NARROW BENCHES ON CONTOUR JOB.
authors: Mason R.
abstract: Maneuvering equipment efficiently on narrow benches encountered in contour stripping is a big problem. But Pratt Mining Co. , Kingston, WV, is solving it with a newly purchased hydraulic front shovel. The shovel can dig out overburden and parting from essentially one position, thus relieving congested traffic on the narrow benches, and can also operate close to the outslope without spilling material down the slope - a practice prohibited by surface mining regulations. Pratt Mining adopted contour stripping to maximize recovery of the high quality metallurgical coal and to minimize overburden removal. The easy maneuverability of the hydraulic front shovel makes it effective for both stripping overburden and removing coal.

title: COST MODEL FOR REMOTE INSPECTION OF GROUND SITES.
authors: Maxim L.; Cullen D.
abstract: A simple model is developed to assess the cost/effectiveness of remote sensing for inspection of ground activities with application to the inspection of surface mining operations. The model considers both single and multiple tier systems (those in which additional inspection is conducted if a higher order tier indicates a violation), possible trade-offs between alpha and beta errors, the worth of technological improvement, an certain fixed cost aspects of manned inspection. An interesting conclusion of this analysis is that (with current cost factors) satellite and aircraft inspection systems can be cost/effective even with relatively high (0. 15-0. 25) alpha and beta errors.

abstract: After an outline of noise and vibration produced in surface mining, control procedures are outlined. The following reommendations are given. Particle velocities below 2 in. per second greatly reduce the possibility of structural damage as well as noise propagation. Delay caps of greater than eight ms should be used in association with a sequential blasting machine under controlled conditions. Adequate burden and stemming should be utilized to prevent the premature escape of by product gases. Minimization of the height of exposed faces should reduce the effects of air blast caused by face movement. Detonation cord should be buried by one to two ft. of dirt or sand, or low energy detonation cord should be used. Blasting should be restricted if weather conditions are likely to cause down range focusing of air blast waves. Blast frequency should be minimized. Blasting should be timed to coincide with the highest ambient noise level of the immediate area. Notification of residents of blasting times should minimize the element of surprise. Public relations efforts should be increased to educate the general public in blasting procedures and in resultant vibrations and noise effects.

title: PLANNING OF A NEW SURFACE MINE - WESTERN COAL.

abstract: There are five geological provinces in the western states from which 100 percent of the lignite and sub-bituminous coal comes. Part of just one province, the Northern Great Plains, has recoverable reserves of lignite and sub-bituminous and bituminous coal which account for 44 percent of the nation's total. title: CAN SURFACE MINING BE COMPATIBLE WITH URBANIZATION?
authors: Coates W.E.
abstract: The compatibility or social acceptability of surface mining in and near urban areas is investigated at two points in time: (1) during the active extraction period and (2) after completion of extraction. Those features which make the typical surface mining operation quite dissimilar to normal urban uses are examined with respect to the objections usually raised by neighboring, nonextractive land owners. Means of amelioration available to the operator to mitigate the adverse impacts causing the objections are examined. Compatibility versus urbanization is investigated in terms of after-use potential. The consideration of extractive operations as ″interim″ land uses is investigated in a variety of site situations. Variations in time of after-use planning, with respect to the age of the operation and ″futuristic″ after-use potential, are investigated through case-study examples and schematic-study proposals.

abstract: Australia has now become the world's largest producer of bauxite, and total production is still rising. Only 20 years ago, the country'S output was virtually negligible. Much of this rapid progress can be attributed to the high-grade discoveries at Weipa, in the Cape York peninsula area, the site of what is already the world's greatest single bauxite producer, with further excellent prospects for increases in production. Weipa has also proved to be the cornerstone for the very rapid development of a substantial proportion of Australia's own domestic aluminum industry. Geology of the orebody estimated to contain 520-million tons grading between 52 and 60% Al//2O//3 that cover a 73 sq mi area and of further 230 sq mi areas estimated to contain some 1,700-million tons of bauxite with grades of between 45 and 58% Al//2O//3 is described. Surface mining operations are removing an average 3 ft of overburden and are using wheel mounted, diesel operated, front end loaders that deliver straight to the haul trucks. Grade control, beneficiation, calcining plants, as well as railway and port facilities are described.

In each case geological, mining and data processing staff have been involved in design and control.

title: Digging into mine waste
abstract: In the U.S., mining activities now affect approximately 13 million acres, or about 0.5% of the total U.S. land area. Of this total, 7 million have been undercut, 3 million disturbed by surface mining, and 3 million given over to mining related waste accumulations. The subject of mining related environmental pollution is discussed and some of the possible remedial measures for the reparation of environmental damage are considered. Because of aquifer and stream disruption, both coal and hard rock mines give rise to water pollution from mine drainage, both acid and alkaline. The polluting effects of solid waste production through disposal of mine tailing after mineral values are extracted, such as land slides, air pollution through dust blowoff, and smoldering from spontaneous combustion, are also discussed. Some of the more effective methods of restoring environmental damage and meeting Federal pollution control standards are reviewed.

title: EQUIPMENT NEEDS TO MEET THE CHLLENGE OF SURFACE MINING OF COAL AND URANIUM IN THE DECADE AHEAD.
authors: Ritchie M.
abstract: This paper focuses on the 1975-1985 period in attempting to demonstrate the equipment requirements in the coal and uranium industries for that period. In the coal industry, it appears that both stripping and mining equipment needs will grow at a rate of 10-12%/year in the future. This equipment will not be radially different from that used today even though some increases in size will probably occur in some equipment lines. The emphasis will be upon improvement in present generation machinery. The same may also be true in the uranium industry. Growth rates on the order of perhaps 50%/year will be experienced as the utility industry continues to install plants using nuclear fuels. It appears that ost of the equipment will besimilar to that used today.

title: Limiting Characteristic Data of Steel-Cable-Reinforced Conveyor Belts.
authors: Lachmann H.
abstract: In surface mining operations at the lignite district of Cologne, West Germany, steel-cable-reinforced conveyor belting with an ultimate tensile strength of 5400 kp/cm (over 100 tons/cm of width) is being used. Should conveying be introduced on a larger scale in the future to relieve transportation of bulk materials by road, rail, or water, much larger installations would be needed. Paper analyzes the limitations involved in construction of this type of belting, weight of belts, vulcanization techniques, required width of the belt for various tensile strength, as well as in drives, and concludes that the ultimate tensile strength of 10,000 kp/cm (about 200 tons/cm of width) appears to be the limit.

title: Evaluation of coal mine methane inventory methods using aircraft-based approaches in the Bowen Basin, Australia
authors: Harris S.J.; Krautwurst S.; Hacker J.; Lunt M.; Borchardt J.; Bai M.; Boesch H.; Brain T.; Burrows J.P.; Chakravarty S.; Field R.A.; Fisher R.E.; France J.L.; Gerilowski K.; Huhs O.; Junkermann W.; Kelly B.F.J.; Kumm M.; Lanoisellé M.; Lieff W.; McGrath A.; Murphy A.; Röckmann T.; Salmon Z.; Schindewolf J.; Thoböll J.; van der Veen C.; Bovensmann H.
abstract: Australia uses a blend of IPCC Tier 2 and 3 bottom-up approaches to estimate and report fugitive coal mine methane (CH<inf>4</inf>) emissions. To date, Tier 3 reporting for underground coal mines, which predominantly relies on direct measurements of ventilated air, has not been systematically assessed against top-down atmospheric measurements. Tier 2 coal core-based emission factors and Tier 3 model guidelines for estimating surface (open-cut) mine emissions similarly lack verification. Here, an in-situ and a remote sensing aircraft-based approach were used to quantify CH<inf>4</inf> emission rates from 17 coal mines in the Bowen Basin, Australia. When compared to bottom-up mean annual reported estimates, airborne estimates from underground mines showed a non-significant mean positive bias of 0.28 t h<sup>−1</sup> (p = 0.28,n = 8 estimates) and good agreement (normalised root mean squared error (NRMSE) = 0.20). When aggregated, top-down measured emissions from all underground mines were within 8 % of bottom-up reported totals. In contrast, aircraft-based estimates from surface mines showed a significant mean positive bias of 3.7 t h<sup>−1</sup> CH<inf>4</inf> (p = 0.001,n = 10 estimates) and poor agreement (NRMSE = 0.86). In aggregate, top-down emissions from all surface mines were 3.6 times the bottom-up totals. Alignment between airborne top-down and measured vented underground coal mine emissions increases confidence in Australia’s Tier 3 direct monitoring methods, while the difference between top-down and bottom-up surface mine emission estimates suggests core-based methods require review. Given that surface mines in the Basin alone account for ∼ 38 % of national production, the contribution of coal mining to Australia’s CH<inf>4</inf> emissions may exceed the reported ∼ 19 %.
